output.brief: The overtime overrun comes mainly from closing work, not from the hiring freeze. From 1 April the closing contract (about $96k a year) lapsed. Maintenance staff took over nightly closing at 41 sites as call-backs, each paid at a 3-hour minimum for a 30–45 minute round. Call-back pay rose from $38k to $289k. 1,962 of the 2,295 call-backs are closing entries, and none are in Summit Hill, which kept its contract. Holdover overtime hours were up only 1.5%. Vacancies don't explain the pattern. Eastgate has 1 of 30 positions vacant, yet its overtime roughly doubled. Summit Hill has 5 of 24 vacant, and its overtime is nearly flat. Vacancies and overtime moved together over the year, but the timing and the districts point to the contract change. Internal Audit checked lock logs against the claims and found no padding. Disciplining the two workers would be wrong. The hot-summer explanation is not supported by the pay-code data. Recommend restoring contracted closing, either by an emergency extension or a re-tender, and tracking call-back spending afterward. Don't impose a blanket overtime cap, because the closings are required for liability coverage. Don't discipline anyone yet. The Eastgate favoritism claim is unresolved, since the sign-up sheets were discarded. Keep them from now on and review how closings are allocated. The injury link to overtime is unproven until payroll hours are matched to claims.
